snippet.title: How Outlaw Biker Gangs (The Mongols) Actually Work | How Crime Works | Insider
snippet.description:
Billy Queen was an undercover agent for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. He spent almost three years embedded in the Mongols Motorcycle club.

Queen speaks to Business Insider about the internal workings of the Mongols, how he rose to become an officer in the club, its hierarchy, its rules, and its war with the Hells Angels. In 2000, his infiltration led to the arrest and conviction of 53 members.

Queen also covers his upbringing as the son of an ATF agent and his military service in Vietnam with the 82nd Airborne Division and Special Forces, which he completed before joining the ATF. He describes the training and skills required for undercover work, emphasizing that it is an innate talent more than a learned skill.

Queen is the author of "Under and Alone: Infiltrating the World’s Most Violent Motorcycle Gang" and "Armed and Dangerous: The Hunt for One of America’s Most Wanted Criminals."

snippet.description:
Elizabeth Bigley, born in 1857 in Ontario, Canada, lived many lives — each more daring than the last. To bankers, she was Cassie Chadwick, the mysterious heiress to steel magnate Andrew Carnegie’s fortune. To society, she was a charming widow with endless wealth and refined manners. In truth, she was one of the most brilliant con artists of the early 20th century — a woman who convinced America’s richest institutions that she was destined to inherit millions.

At the height of her deception, Chadwick secured enormous loans from banks and financiers who believed she held promissory notes signed by Carnegie himself. Her word — and a forged document or two — was all it took to unlock fortunes. She used the money to fill mansions with European art, gold, and jewels, living as one of the most extravagant women of her time.

When the truth finally surfaced in 1904, the public was stunned. There were no inheritance papers, no secret trust, and no connection to Carnegie at all. What she left behind was not wealth, but chaos — bankers ruined, investors humiliated, and reputations destroyed. The Cleveland Carnegie Hoax, as newspapers called it, became one of the earliest and most infamous cases of financial fraud in American history.

• The genius behind her fake Carnegie connection and forged promissory notes

snippet.title: Carmine Galante: The Don Who Brought the Heroin Empire to America | Gangster Sleep Story
snippet.description:
Carmine “Lilo” Galante, born in 1910 in East Harlem, New York, was one of the most ruthless and ambitious figures the American Mafia ever produced. Cold, calculating, and unflinchingly violent, Galante rose through the ranks of the Bonanno crime family with one goal — total control of the heroin trade. His dream, and his obsession, would reshape the underworld and unleash the infamous “French Connection” — a billion-dollar drug pipeline that flooded America with narcotics.

Known for his piercing stare and ever-present cigar, Galante’s reputation for brutality made even seasoned mobsters uneasy. He carried out murders for the Mafia Commission, built alliances with Sicilian traffickers, and operated with a level of arrogance that defied the old rules. By the 1970s, he effectively ruled the Bonanno family, positioning himself as the “Godfather of Heroin.”

But Galante’s rise came with enemies — both inside and outside his family. His defiance of the Commission and hunger for dominance over the drug trade sealed his fate. On a warm afternoon in July 1979, while dining at an Italian restaurant in Brooklyn, Galante’s reign ended abruptly — assassinated by men he once called his own. His cigar was still between his teeth.

snippet.title: How NASA Astronauts Actually Work | Authorized Account | Insider
snippet.description:
Mike Massimino is a former NASA astronaut and veteran of two Space Shuttle missions.

Massimino began his career as an engineer working at IBM and McDonnell Douglas Aerospace after earning degrees from Columbia University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He applied to NASA three times before being selected as an astronaut in 1996. He went on to fly two Space Shuttle missions, in 2002 and 2009, both focused on servicing the Hubble Space Telescope. During these missions, he performed multiple space walks and was part of a team that set a record for total spacewalking time on a single shuttle mission.

He talks to Business Insider about astronaut training and recruitment, as well as daily life in space, including how astronauts eat, drink, and sleep. He also discusses becoming the first person to tweet from space and shares his perspective on the future of human spaceflight, including the Artemis II mission.

After leaving NASA, Massimino became a professor of mechanical engineering at Columbia University, and he acts as a senior advisor for space programs at the Intrepid Museum. He has made numerous television appearances, including a recurring role as himself on "The Big Bang Theory."
